nameStory: Sacred datura earned its mystical name from Native American tribes of the Southwest, who considered this powerful plant sacred and used it in religious ceremonies. The word 'datura' comes from the Hindi 'dhatura,' while 'sacred' reflects the deep spiritual significance this plant held for indigenous peoples who understood both its power and its dangers.
description: Sacred datura is a striking perennial plant with large, trumpet-shaped white flowers that seem almost otherworldly in their beauty. This southwestern native can grow 3-5 feet tall and wide, forming a sprawling, bushy mound. In New England, you'll only encounter it as an ornamental garden plant, since our cold winters prevent it from surviving naturally. The plant belongs to the nightshade family and is extremely poisonous in all parts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Massive white trumpet-shaped blooms, 6-8 inches long, that open in evening with an intoxicating sweet fragrance that attracts night-flying moths

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, soft gray-green leaves with a velvety, almost fuzzy texture that feel thick and substantial when touched, arranged alternately on stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive spiny, egg-shaped seed pods about 2 inches across, covered in sharp thorns that split open when ripe to reveal dark seeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a sprawling, rounded shrub-like mound that spreads wider than it is tall, with thick, somewhat succulent-looking stems

habitat: In New England, sacred datura is found only in cultivated gardens, particularly specialty or botanical gardens that grow southwestern plants. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, often planted in xerophytic (dry-loving) garden sections or desert plant collections. You might spot it at conservatories or in private gardens of plant enthusiasts.

seasonality.spring: Young plants may be set out in gardens after frost danger passes, showing their distinctive fuzzy gray-green foliage as they establish.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with the spectacular large white trumpets opening in evening and closing by morning, followed by the development of spiny seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in warm years, with mature spiny fruits splitting open to release seeds before plants are killed by frost.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely in New England's freezing temperatures, surviving only as seeds or in heated greenhouses.

funFact: Sacred datura flowers are nature's night shift workers - they open only in the evening and close by morning, perfectly timed to attract their primary pollinators, hawkmoths, which hover like hummingbirds while drinking nectar in the darkness.
confusionNotes: The large trumpet flowers might remind you of morning glories, but sacred datura's blooms are much larger, white (not colorful), open at night (not morning), and the plants have very different fuzzy, thick leaves instead of heart-shaped thin ones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beauty, sacred datura is extremely dangerous - all parts contain powerful toxic alkaloids that can cause hallucinations, delirium, and death. Never handle without gloves and keep away from children and pets. This is a plant to admire from a distance only.
compareHints: Sacred datura differs from its relative jimsonweed (the only other Datura commonly found in New England) by having much larger flowers, gray-green fuzzy leaves instead of bright green smooth ones, and a perennial growth habit rather than being an annual. Jimsonweed also has purple-tinged flowers sometimes, while sacred datura flowers are pure white.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Jimsonweed is the most common Datura species in New England, distinguished from its relatives by its upward-facing white flowers and especially spiny seed pods.
Metel devil's trumpet has larger, more ornamental upward-facing flowers compared to its weedy cousin jimsonweed, which has smaller white or purple flowers and more deeply toothed leaves.
Unlike its cousin jimsonweed which has smooth leaves and upright white flowers, downy thorn-apple has that distinctive fuzzy texture and flowers that nod slightly downward.
